Standard Errors that Account for Estimated Weights (M-estimation)

Source: R/ipwvcov.R
ipwvcov.Rd

Experimental: this function is new in ipw 1.4.0. Its interface and output may change in future versions, and the methods are still being evaluated. The bootstrap, re-estimating the weights in each bootstrap sample, remains the established alternative, especially with heavy-tailed weights.

Variance-covariance matrix of the coefficients of a marginal structural model fitted with lm(), glm() or survival::coxph() and weights from ipwpoint for a binary point treatment, or with time-varying weights from ipwtm, taking the estimation of the weights into account. The marginal structural model and the exposure models are treated as one set of stacked estimating equations (M-estimation; Lunceford & Davidian 2004), and the sandwich variance of all parameters is computed; the block for the coefficients of the marginal structural model is returned.

Usage

ipwvcov(object, msm)

Arguments

object

Result of ipwpoint with family = "binomial" and link = "logit"; or result of ipwtm with family = "binomial" and link = "logit"; or a list of ipwtm() (and ipwpoint()) results whose weights multiply to the weights of msm.

msm

Marginal structural model: an lm, glm or coxph fit with weights equal to object$ipw.weights (or their product for a list), on the same rows in the same order as the data given to ipwpoint() or ipwtm().

Value

Variance-covariance matrix of the coefficients of msm, with the coefficient names as row and column names. It can be passed, for example, to lmtest::coeftest(msm, vcov. = ...).

Details

Robust (sandwich) standard errors of a weighted model, such as those from svyglm() or sandwich::vcovHC(), treat the weights as known. Here the estimating equations of the denominator (and numerator) model are stacked under those of the marginal structural model. With \(\theta = (\beta, \alpha, \gamma)\) the coefficients of the marginal structural model, the denominator model and the numerator model, and \(\psi_i(\theta)\) the contribution of person \(i\) to the stacked estimating equations, the variance is \(A^{-1} B A^{-T}\) with \(A = -\sum_i \partial \psi_i / \partial \theta\) and \(B = \sum_i \psi_i \psi_i^T\), evaluated at the estimates. The derivative of each weight with respect to the exposure-model coefficients is worked out for each estimand (ATE, ATT, ATC, ATO). The exposure models must use the logit link: the information matrices use the expected (Fisher) information, which equals the observed information, and so gives the exact sandwich, only for canonical links. For the marginal structural model any glm() link is accepted. With a non-canonical link (for example a log link for risk ratios) and a saturated model such as y ~ a for the binary exposure, the expected and observed information are exactly equal in any sample: the fitted mean in each exposure group is that group's weighted mean of y, so the extra term of the observed information, a weighted sum of residuals times a factor that is constant within each group, sums to zero within each group. For other models with a non-canonical link the two are asymptotically equivalent when the model is correctly specified. No small-sample correction is applied. Proportional rescaling of the weights does not change the result.

Cox models. For a coxph() marginal structural model the weighted partial likelihood score is used as the estimating equation (Binder 1992; Lin & Wei 1989), with the Breslow form for tied event times. Person \(i\)'s contribution is \(w_i\) times the score residual, \(U_i = w_i [\delta_i (X_i - \bar X(t_i)) - \sum_k \delta_k w_k Y_i(t_k) e^{\beta' X_i} (X_i - \bar X(t_k)) / S_0(t_k)]\), with \(S_0(t) = \sum_j w_j Y_j(t) e^{\beta' X_j}\) and \(\bar X(t)\) the weighted mean of \(X\) in the risk set; residuals(msm, type = "score") returns the part in brackets (without the weight). The bread for \(\beta\) is the weighted information matrix (the inverse of msm$naive.var). The weights enter both each person's own term and the risk-set sums; differentiating the total score with respect to one weight gives exactly that person's score residual, so the cross block is \(-\sum_i U_i d_i^T\) with \(d_i = \partial \log w_i / \partial \alpha\), as for glm(). It is computed analytically; the package tests check it against central finite differences of the stacked estimating equations. Without the exposure models, the sandwich reduces to coxph()'s robust variance (msm$var), which treats the weights as known.

Supported: object from ipwpoint(family = "binomial", link = "logit") with denominator (and, if present, numerator) models fitted by glm() (no smooth terms) and any estimand; msm of class "lm" or "glm", fitted on the same rows, in the same order, as the weights, with weights = object$ipw.weights; or msm from coxph() with right-censored data Surv(time, status), one row per person in the same order, and the same weights. For coxph(), tied event times need ties = "breslow"; without tied event times all tie methods give the same result.

Time-varying weights. object can be an ipwtm() result, or a list of ipwtm() (and ipwpoint()) results whose ipw.weights multiply to the weights of msm, typically treatment weights times censoring weights. Each model is a separate parameter block. The unit of independence is the subject (the id of ipwtm()): all scores are summed within subject before the meat \(B = \sum_{subjects} \psi_p \psi_p^T\) is formed. The weight of row \(r\) is the product, over the rows \(s \le r\) of the same subject, of numerator over denominator factors \(f_s\), as defined by ipwtm(): \(P(A_s = a_s)\) for type = "first" and "all", \(1 - p_s\) for type = "cens" (the censoring row included), and 1 after the first switch. With logistic models, \(\partial \log f_s / \partial \alpha\) is \((a_s - p_s) Z_s\) ("first", "all") or \(-p_s Z_s\) ("cens"), so \(d_r = \partial \log w_r / \partial \alpha\) is minus the cumulative sum of these over the rows used by the model, within subject in time order (plus, for the numerator). The cross block is \(-\sum_r U_r d_r^T\) for lm(), glm() and Cox models; for a Cox model on counting-process data Surv(tstart, time, event) the identity above holds row by row, because each row enters the risk sets with its own weight. Without the exposure models the sandwich reduces to the cluster-robust variance that treats the weights as known (for a Cox model, coxph() with cluster(id)).

Supported for time-varying weights: ipwtm(family = "binomial", link = "logit") with any type, glm models without smooth terms, no truncation, made with this version of ipw; msm fitted with lm(), glm() or coxph() (counting-process data; cluster() is allowed, ties = "breslow" when event times are tied) on all rows of the long data, in the same order, with weights equal to the product of the weights in object.

Heavy-tailed weights. Cumulative weights can have a heavy right tail when some people have a very low probability of their observed exposure history (a near-violation of positivity). Normal-theory intervals are then unreliable whatever method gives the standard error, the bootstrap included. In simulations where treatment depended strongly on the confounder and on past treatment, the tail index of the final cumulative weights was about 2.3 (the weights have a finite variance, but not a finite third or fourth moment). The mean variance from ipwvcov() was then 0.84 to 0.93 times the true variance of the estimates (the standard error 3 to 8% too small), and 95% intervals covered 92 to 93% of the time, with no trend towards 95% between 300 and 4800 people. The cluster bootstrap did no better (variance ratio 0.86 to 1.00 on fewer data sets, coverage 90 to 95%). With a tail index of about 3.9 the variance ratios were 1.05 (ipwvcov()) and 1.04 (bootstrap), and both covered 95.8% and 96.5% of the time. Check the weight distribution (summary(), ipwplot and the effective sample size sum(w)^2 / sum(w^2)) before trusting any standard error.

Not supported, and an error: other exposure families or links, smooth terms (GAMs), truncated weights (truncation at estimated percentiles is not a smooth function of the model coefficients), ipwtm() weights from Cox (family = "survival"), multinomial, ordinal or gaussian models, and coxph() models with strata(), frailty() or tt() terms, or Efron or exact ties with tied event times. With ipwpoint() weights the coxph() model must have right-censored data (one row per person) and no cluster(); with ipwtm() weights it must have counting-process data. Use the bootstrap there, re-estimating the weights in each bootstrap sample (see ipwpoint and vignette("ipw"); for long data, the cluster bootstrap that resamples subjects).

This is the same kind of standard error as vcov = "asympt" in WeightIt::glm_weightit(); in the package tests the two agree for binary treatments. For Cox models, ipwvcov() agrees with a numerical Jacobian of the stacked estimating equations to about \(10^{-7}\). WeightIt::coxph_weightit(vcov = "asympt") gives slightly different values: for the ATE and overlap weights the relative difference was below 0.1% and shrank with the sample size; for ATT and ATC weights its standard error was 1 to 4% larger and the difference did not shrink. Its vcov = "HC0" equals coxph()'s robust variance exactly.

References

Lunceford, J.K. & Davidian, M. (2004). Stratification and weighting via the propensity score in estimation of causal treatment effects: a comparative study. Statistics in Medicine, 23, 2937-2960. doi:10.1002/sim.1903 .

Binder, D.A. (1992). Fitting Cox's proportional hazards models from survey data. Biometrika, 79, 139-147. doi:10.1093/biomet/79.1.139 .

Lin, D.Y. & Wei, L.J. (1989). The robust inference for the Cox proportional hazards model. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 84, 1074-1078. doi:10.1080/01621459.1989.10478874 .

Stefanski, L.A. & Boos, D.D. (2002). The calculus of M-estimation. The American Statistician, 56, 29-38. doi:10.1198/000313002753631330 .

Greifer, N. WeightIt: Weighting for Covariate Balance in Observational Studies. R package, https://ngreifer.github.io/WeightIt/. (Its glm_weightit(vcov = "asympt") is used in the package tests as an independent comparison.)

See also

ipwpoint, ipwtm

Examples

# Moderate confounding, so the weights are well behaved (check them with
# ipwdiag() before trusting any standard error). True effect of a: 1.
set.seed(2026)
n <- 1000
simdat <- data.frame(l = rnorm(n))
simdat$a <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.2 + 0.6 * simdat$l))
simdat$y <- 1 + 1 * simdat$a + 0.8 * simdat$l + rnorm(n)

w <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
              numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = simdat)
msm <- lm(y ~ a, data = simdat, weights = w$ipw.weights)

# standard errors that account for the estimated weights
sqrt(diag(ipwvcov(w, msm)))
#> (Intercept)           a 
#>  0.04944754  0.06540414 

# overlap weights
w.ato <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  denominator = ~ l, data = simdat, estimand = "ATO")
msm.ato <- lm(y ~ a, data = simdat, weights = w.ato$ipw.weights)
sqrt(diag(ipwvcov(w.ato, msm.ato)))
#> (Intercept)           a 
#>  0.04913073  0.06295543 

# Wald tests and confidence intervals
if (requireNamespace("lmtest", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(lmtest::coeftest(msm, vcov. = ipwvcov(w, msm)))
  print(lmtest::coefci(msm, vcov. = ipwvcov(w, msm)))
}
#> 
#> t test of coefficients:
#> 
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value  Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept) 1.049651   0.049448  21.228 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> a           0.934934   0.065404  14.295 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#>                 2.5 %   97.5 %
#> (Intercept) 0.9526177 1.146684
#> a           0.8065889 1.063280

# Cox marginal structural model for a survival outcome
library(survival)
simdat$time <- rexp(n, 0.1 * exp(-0.5 * simdat$a + 0.5 * simdat$l))
simdat$status <- as.numeric(simdat$time < 10)
simdat$time <- pmin(simdat$time, 10)
msm.cox <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ a, data = simdat, weights = w$ipw.weights)
cbind(robust = sqrt(diag(msm.cox$var)),          # weights treated as known
      ipwvcov = sqrt(diag(ipwvcov(w, msm.cox))))  # weights estimated
#>       robust    ipwvcov
#> a 0.09201763 0.08487011

# Time-varying weights: treatment (type = "first") times censoring
# (type = "cens") weights from pooled logistic models, and a Cox MSM on
# the long data
data(haartdat)
w.haart <- ipwtm(exposure = haartind, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                 numerator = ~ sex + age, denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
                 id = patient, timevar = fuptime, type = "first", data = haartdat)
w.cens <- ipwtm(exposure = dropout, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                numerator = ~ sex + age, denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
                id = patient, timevar = fuptime, type = "cens", data = haartdat)
msm.haart <- coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind + cluster(patient),
                   data = haartdat, ties = "breslow",
                   weights = w.haart$ipw.weights * w.cens$ipw.weights)
cbind(robust.cluster = sqrt(diag(msm.haart$var)),
      ipwvcov = sqrt(diag(ipwvcov(list(w.haart, w.cens), msm.haart))))
#>          robust.cluster   ipwvcov
#> haartind      0.4633263 0.4585489
